content: Azithromycin for injection, marketed as ZITHROMAX, is specifically indicated for the treatment of infections caused by susceptible strains of designated microorganisms in the conditions outlined below. The recommended dosages, durations of therapy, and applicable patient populations vary depending on the specific infection. For detailed dosing recommendations, refer to the Dosage and Administration section. 1. Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP): ZITHROMAX is indicated for the treatment of community-acquired pneumonia caused by Chlamydia pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Legionella pneumophila, Moraxella catarrhalis, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, or Streptococcus pneumoniae in patients who require initial intravenous therapy. 2. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID): ZITHROMAX is indicated for the treatment of pelvic inflammatory disease caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, or Mycoplasma hominis in patients who require initial intravenous therapy. If anaerobic microorganisms are suspected to contribute to the infection, an antimicrobial agent with anaerobic activity should be administered in combination with ZITHROMAX. 3. Transition to Oral Therapy: Following initial intravenous administration, ZITHROMAX should be transitioned to oral administration as clinically indicated. Refer to the Dosage and Administration section for further guidance. 4. Microbiological Testing: Prior to initiating treatment, appropriate culture and susceptibility tests should be performed to identify the causative microorganism and its susceptibility to azithromycin. However, therapy with ZITHROMAX may be initiated before the results of these tests are available. Once the results are obtained, antimicrobial therapy should be adjusted accordingly. 5. Antimicrobial Stewardship: To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the efficacy of ZITHROMAX and other antibacterial agents, ZITHROMAX should only be used to treat or prevent infections that are proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. When culture and susceptibility data are available, they should guide the selection or modification of antibacterial therapy. In the absence of such data, local epidemiological and susceptibility patterns should be considered to inform empiric therapy selection.
